title: Cooperation in the band; his Chicago interviews by instrument
summary: Russell says working together is the core of New Orleans style and describes interviewing Baby Dodds, Omer Simeon, Roy Palmer and Natty Dominique.

story.theme_name: Drummers and drumming: who played what, and how
story.community_name: Great drummers: who they admired and why

blocks.x: Or else it's the type of people that, for one thing, one of the great principles which you can't really overemphasize in New Orleans music, in the jazz, is the working together. The way they can work together. They're all there to help one another, as they say. They'll, they're not there to steal the spotlight. They're always there trying to help somebody misses a note or they can see they're falling down on their part. They'll put in notes that'll fill in or they'll, I mean, it's not quite that simple, but I mean it's that spirit that the musicians do work together. That's one of the main principles that's made New Orleans music what it is. Everybody talks about the ensemble style as opposed to solo style, but that's a part of it, that working together and the friendly spirit. And yet some of the bands sometimes can get in sort of fights too. You'll find a lot of that goes on even here, but not as much as other, other places. You mean within the band? Within the band. Not nearly as much. And they're a good band that really is playing well together there. As Baby Dodd says, you have to be friendly, you have to be happy. Incidentally, that's in a little drum book. Some of that's in his autobiography too. But I have a little drum book which I hope someday will be published, maybe as a part of a bigger book. I started this work in Chicago of interviewing some of what I consider the outstanding New Orleans musicians on each instrument. To find out what their part in the band is. What they, not necessarily instruction to younger players, but also that would be of value to younger players coming up that wanted to take up New Orleans style. What they have to do, what they have to learn to play the New Orleans style. So up there in Chicago I'd interviewed Baby Dodds quite a few interviews, as well as some of his music, demonstrating the drums and different traps as they call them. Also, Omer Simeon, who was certainly one of the outstanding New Orleans clarinetists, although he didn't play hardly, I guess, at all down here. But he was a member of Jelly Rolls band up there, and Jelly considered him the greatest clarinetist he'd ever worked with.
He was my favorite of all of them on my own record.

And then also, not that I was just trying to pick Jelly's favorite musicians, but Roy Palmer, whom Jelly also considered the best trombonist. Who had only recorded one very early date with Jelly on an old autograph session. But I had a good interview with him. And also Natty Dominick, who maybe wasn't one of the two or three greatest all-time trumpet players, but certainly had a wonderful rhythmic driving style. One of the choice men as far as personally a wonderful fellow.
